disguised_difficulty: L6 carries essentially all remaining difficulty after normalization and cyclotomic bookkeeping. This is acceptable because it is explicitly isolated as the bottleneck rather than hidden inside a routine-looking support lemma.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix arbitrary integers n, k, l with 0 <= k, l <= n and assume [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is a polynomial. First use Gaussian symmetry to replace k and l by a = min(k, n-k) and b = min(l, n-l), so both reduced indices lie in [0, n/2]. A degree comparison then rules out a < b, because a quotient with smaller reduced numerator index would have negative degree and could not be a polynomial. With a >= b, rewrite the reduced quotient as an interval product Q_{A,B,d}(q) = prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)). Next compute the exponent of each cyclotomic polynomial Phi_m(q) in Q_{A,B,d}(q); it is exactly the floor-difference e_m attached to the two intervals. Since the original quotient is assumed to be a polynomial, the general cyclotomic criterion forces every exponent e_m to be nonnegative. The only genuine hard input is then the reduced interval-product positivity theorem L6, which says that these nonnegative exponent inequalities imply coefficientwise nonnegativity of Q_{A,B,d}(q). Substituting back through the normal-form identity yields the desired positivity for [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q.

steps.trivial_justification: Apply L1 once with r = k and once with r = l. The definition of minimum gives a <= n/2 and b <= n/2.

steps.trivial_justification: By A1, the original quotient equals [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q and is a polynomial by hypothesis. If a < b, then 0 <= a < b <= n/2, so L2 says [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q cannot lie in Q[q]. This contradicts the hypothesis. Therefore a >= b.

steps.derives: Define d := a-b, A := n-a, and B := b. Then d >= 0 and A >= B >= 0, and the original quotient can be written as [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q = Q_{A,B,d}(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)).
steps.trivial_justification: A1 rewrites the quotient as [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q. Since A2 gives 0 <= b <= a <= n/2, the hypotheses of L3 hold, so L3 converts that reduced quotient into the interval product Q_{A,B,d}(q). Also A = n-a >= a >= b = B.

steps.derives: The rational function Q_{A,B,d}(q) belongs to Q[q].
steps.trivial_justification: By A3, Q_{A,B,d}(q) is exactly the original quotient, and the theorem hypothesis states that the original quotient is a polynomial in q.

steps.derives: For each positive integer m, the exponent of Phi_m(q) in the cyclotomic factorization of Q_{A,B,d}(q) is e_m = floor((A+d)/m) - floor(A/m) - floor((B+d)/m) + floor(B/m).
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L4 directly to the interval product Q_{A,B,d}(q) obtained in A3.

steps.trivial_justification: L6 applies to the same parameters A, B, d because A3 gives A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, while A6 verifies the hypothesis e_m >= 0 for every positive integer m.

Consequently, if 0 <= a < b <= n/2, then the rational function [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q has negative degree and therefore does not belong to the polynomial ring Q[q].

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Computes the cyclotomic exponent data attached to the interval product.
lemmas.statement_nl: For integers A, B, d with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, define Q_{A,B,d}(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)). Let Phi_m(q) be the m-th cyclotomic polynomial, characterized by 1 - q^N = prod_{m | N} Phi_m(q). Then Q_{A,B,d}(q) = prod_{m >= 1} Phi_m(q)^(e_m), where all but finitely many e_m are zero and e_m = #{x in {A+1,...,A+d} : m divides x} - #{x in {B+1,...,B+d} : m divides x} = floor((A+d)/m) - floor(A/m) - floor((B+d)/m) + floor(B/m).

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Converts the polynomiality hypothesis into nonnegativity of all cyclotomic exponents.
lemmas.statement_nl: Let e : Z_{>0} -> Z be a finitely supported integer-valued function, and define F(q) := prod_{m >= 1} Phi_m(q)^(e(m)) in the rational function field Q(q), where Phi_m(q) is the m-th cyclotomic polynomial. Then F(q) lies in Q[q] if and only if e(m) >= 0 for every positive integer m. In that case F(q) actually lies in Z[q].

lemmas.role_in_assembly: This is the reduced core positivity theorem for interval quotients, which completes the proof after all easy reductions.
lemmas.statement_nl: For integers A, B, d with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, define Q_{A,B,d}(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)), and for each positive integer m define e_m := floor((A+d)/m) - floor(A/m) - floor((B+d)/m) + floor(B/m). If e_m >= 0 for every positive integer m, then Q_{A,B,d}(q) belongs to Z[q], and every coefficient of that polynomial is nonnegative.

payload.theorem_nl: Let [n choose k]_q denote the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient. Prove that for all integers n, k, l with 0 ≤ k, l ≤ n, if [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is a polynomial in q, then that polynomial has only nonnegative coefficients.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix arbitrary integers n, k, l with 0 <= k, l <= n and assume that R(q) := [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q lies in Q[q]. First use Gaussian symmetry to replace k and l by a := min(k, n-k) and b := min(l, n-l), so the quotient becomes [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q with 0 <= a, b <= n/2. A degree comparison shows that a cannot be smaller than b; otherwise the reduced quotient would have negative degree and could not be a polynomial. Now set d := a-b, A := n-a, and B := b. The quotient is then the interval product Q_{A,B,d}(q) = prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)). The central new input is the bottleneck lemma L4: polynomiality of this reduced interval quotient implies the existence of a weighted polynomial ring S = Q[x_1, ..., x_d] with variable weights B+1, ..., B+d and a homogeneous regular sequence of degrees A+1, ..., A+d. By the standard complete-intersection Hilbert-series formula L5, the Hilbert series of S/(f_1, ..., f_d) is exactly the same interval product, hence exactly the original q-binomial quotient. Since positively weighted polynomial rings and their homogeneous quotients have finite-dimensional graded pieces (L7), the Hilbert series lemma L6 shows that every coefficient of this Hilbert series is a nonnegative integer. Therefore the original polynomial quotient has only nonnegative coefficients. Since n, k, and l were arbitrary, this proves the theorem.

From A1, the original quotient equals [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q and is a polynomial by the theorem hypothesis. If a < b, then A1 gives 0 <= a < b <= n/2, so L2 implies that [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q cannot belong to Q[q]. This contradicts the hypothesis. Therefore a >= b.

steps.trivial_justification: A2 gives d = a-b >= 0. Since A1 gives a <= n/2, we have A = n-a >= a, and A2 gives a >= b = B, hence A >= B >= 0. Now apply L3 to the reduced pair (a,b) to rewrite [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q as the displayed interval product. Combining with A1 yields the same formula for the original quotient.
A3 identifies Q_{A,B,d}(q) with the original quotient, and the theorem hypothesis states that the original quotient is a polynomial in q.

steps.trivial_justification: Because the f_i found in A5 are homogeneous, the ideal I they generate is homogeneous. Apply L5 with weights w_i := B+i and degrees e_i := A+i. This gives Hilb_{S/I}(q) = prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)). By A3, that same product is exactly Q_{A,B,d}(q), and A3 also identified Q_{A,B,d}(q) with the original q-binomial quotient.

steps.trivial_justification: The grading weights of S are B+1, ..., B+d, all of which are positive. A6 states that I is a homogeneous ideal of S. Therefore L7 applies and gives finite-dimensionality of every graded piece of the quotient ring S/I.

steps.derives: The formal power series [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q has coefficients in Z_{>=0}; since it is polynomial by hypothesis, that polynomial has only nonnegative coefficients.
steps.trivial_justification: By A7, the graded Q-vector space S/I has finite-dimensional homogeneous pieces, so L6 applies to M := S/I and shows that Hilb_{S/I}(q) has nonnegative integer coefficients. Hence the coefficients of the quotient are all nonnegative; because the theorem hypothesis already says the quotient is a polynomial, this is exactly the desired coefficientwise nonnegativity.

shared_context.content: If w_1, ..., w_d are positive integers, then Q[x_1, ..., x_d] is N-graded by deg(x_i) = w_i. For a graded Q-vector space M = direct sum_{m >= 0} M_m with each M_m finite-dimensional, Hilb_M(q) := sum_{m >= 0} (dim_Q M_m) q^m.
shared_context.label: Weighted grading and Hilbert series

shared_context.content: In a commutative ring R, a sequence f_1, ..., f_t is regular if for each i the image of f_i is not a zero-divisor in R/(f_1, ..., f_{i-1}). The empty sequence is regular.
shared_context.label: Regular sequence

shared_context.content: A polynomial f(q) in Z[q] is coefficientwise nonnegative if every coefficient in its expansion in powers of q is >= 0.
shared_context.label: Coefficientwise nonnegative

shared_context.content: A product over an empty index set is equal to 1.
shared_context.label: Empty product

candidates.strategy_summary: Unlike the previously rejected cyclotomic-exponent route (which had no missing-coverage gaps but concentrated the hard part in a direct positivity theorem), this candidate keeps only the easy symmetry/degree normalization and then switches to a commutative-algebra strategy: a polynomial reduced interval quotient is realized as the Hilbert series of a weighted complete intersection, so nonnegative coefficients come from graded dimensions rather than from cyclotomic positivity.
